newsitem.title: USA: Republicans predict quick penalty for Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Republicans predict quick penalty for Gingrich.

text.p: Republicans Sunday predicted the House ethics committee would decide quickly how to penalise Speaker Newt Gingrich for giving the panel false information, paving the way for his re-election as speaker on Jan. 7.
Republicans rallied behind Gingrich, who is second in line to succeed the president, dismissed the violations as minor and said they would vote unanimously to re-elect him.

Democrats, citing Gingrich's attacks on the ethics of President Clinton and his single-handed campaign that led Democratic House Speaker Jim Wright to resign in disgrace in 1989, said the Georgia Republican should take his own.
Gingrich, often a featured guest on the Sunday television talk shows, remained secluded at his Atlanta home as fellow lawmakers debated his conduct and future.

Gingrich on Saturday admitted "with great sadness" that he provided inaccurate information to the ethics committee. He also accepted responsibility for failing to seek advice on whether a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt foundations for partisan purposes.

The findings, the result of a two-year investigation by a four-member panel of the bipartisan ethics committee, came just two weeks before the House votes on whether Gingrich will be the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.
Republicans have a 20-seat majority in the House.
House Majority Leader Dick Armey, a Texas Republican, said Gingrich made what amounted to a minor oversight, admitted it, and now it was time to get on with the business of governing.

The full 10-member bipartisan committee must decide whether to recommend to the full House any penalty for the violations. Punishments can range from a reprimand to a more severe "censure," all the way up to expulsion from the House.

Armey, speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press," stopped short of predicting the outcome of the panel's vote, but said a vote to censure Gingrich, which would require him to step down as speaker, would be incomensurate with the errors he admitted.

The charges centred on the activities of GOPAC, a political action committee formerly headed by Gingrich, his college course called "Renewing American Civilisation" and the role played by tax-exempt nonprofit foundations.

"I think it will be resolved, certainly before the 7th of January," Armey said. "I do not believe that censure would be appropriate for the errors that were made that the speaker has readily accepted responsibility for."
He was anxious to see the matter resolved: "We need to get this behind us and get on with the serious work before us ... about balancing the budget, improving education and so forth."
Armey and other House leaders said they were confident Gingrich would win re-election.
"He will definitely be re-elected," Armey said.
House Whip David Bonior, Gingrich's chief critic, continued his attacks on Gingrich, saying, "We don't need people in the speaker's chair who lie to Congress."

Bonior, speaking on CNN's "Late Edition with Frank Sesno" said, "I think it's very clear from the report... that the speaker of the House of Representatives lied to the committee on 13 separate occasions over a three-month period."
He said Gingrich used money raised for needy kids to further his political objectives and build his "empire."
Republican David Dreier, of California, responded by saying Bonior was "fixated" on Gingrich and his attacks would jeopardise prospects for bipartisan cooperation in Congress.
Former New York governor Mario Cuomo, also appearing on "Meet the Press," said Gingrich should resign.
"The man lied. He got caught," said Cuomo. "He says, I accept the responsibility, but I don't want to pay any price ... Put your actions where your words are. Step down."

Representative John Conyers, ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, released a statement saying the Justice Department should get involved since there were "serious legal questions at stake."
